rules.description: The previous bar was a huge with-trend bar — range well above the recent average, closing in the top fraction of its own range — so this bar is expected to close above its open. Brooks's daily-bar follow-through claim, stated for daily charts but testable on any timeframe.
rules.pseudocode: (high[1] - low[1]) >= rangeMultiple * average(high - low, rangeLookback)[2] && close[1] > open[1] && (close[1] - low[1]) >= closeFraction * (high[1] - low[1])

complexity.reason: a fresh Average of the range expression plus fixed-offset comparisons

catalog_match.note: Shares the large-range idea with BarRangeAboveStd (std-based, current bar, same both sides) and the close-position idea with CloseRangePosition (current bar), but reads BAR 1 for all three terms and is mirrored.

rules.merge_notes: Carried as a composite deliberately: it is a named Brooks claim ('after a huge bull trend day the next day usually closes above its open') that Brian would want tested exactly as stated, and its three terms all read bar 1, which no combination of the lag-0 catalog rules can express. R04-07 is the same claim ('yesterday was a strong trend-from-open bull day, so today should close above the open') stated against an undefined TrendDay primitive; TP3-12's definition won because it is measurable from bar 1's OHLC alone, which removes R04-07's research grade entirely. Pair with NumBars(1) as the exit to test the book's claim directly, per TP3-12's note. Brooks adds that it may repeat for several days in a row.

rules.description: The bar is a strong trend bar: a with-trend body that is at least F of the bar's range, and both tails no larger than T of the range. Brooks's single-bar test for a breakout bar likely to follow through.
rules.pseudocode: close[0] > open[0] && (close[0] - open[0]) >= bodyFraction * (high[0] - low[0]) && (high[0] - close[0]) <= tailFraction * (high[0] - low[0]) && (open[0] - low[0]) <= tailFraction * (high[0] - low[0])

catalog_match.note: CloseRangePosition tests where the CLOSE sits in the bar's range; this tests the BODY as a fraction of range plus both tails. A shaved-top bull bar with a small body passes CloseRangePosition and fails this rule.

rules.merge_notes: RP1-02 (ranges Part I intro) and R02-01 (ranges ch2 'Signs of Strength in a Breakout') are the same pseudocode character for character; the chapter agents were told to redefine shared primitives per file. Brooks gives no numbers anywhere: bodyFraction readings across the bucket are 0.5 (T04-15), 0.6 (RP1-02, R02-01, V15-05, V15-06, R31-10, T18-05, T21-05, T21-54, T21-55, T08-01) and 0.7 (V00-20, T03-07, R28-01, R28-09); tailFraction 0.15 (RP1-02, R02-01) vs 0.2 (V15-05, V15-06, V15-09). Kept the 0.6 / 0.15 majority as the default; both should be optimized. A `lag` input (as on the catalog's InsideBar) lets the several candidates that test the PRIOR bar (V15-05, R01-07, RP1-06, T04-15) use the same rule at lag 1 instead of a second rule.

rules.description: The last N bars are ALL strong trend bars in the same direction — the bucket's mechanized definition of a Brooks 'spike'. At N=2 it is the agreed always-in flip trigger.
rules.pseudocode: for k in 0..consecutiveBars-1: close[k] > open[k] && (close[k] - open[k]) >= bodyFraction * (high[k] - low[k])

complexity.reason: fixed-length window loop over a single-bar test

catalog_match.note: ConsecutiveUpBars is exactly this rule at bodyFraction = 0 (each bar merely closes above its own open). This adds the body-size requirement, which is the whole content of 'strong'. Author as a separate rule rather than re-parameterizing, since bodyFraction = 0 must keep reproducing ConsecutiveUpBars bit for bit.

rules.merge_notes: Seven chapters define 'spike' as a run of consecutive strong trend bars and every one of them is this loop. Run lengths quoted: 2 (V15-06, V24-27, T21-10 default), 3 (T03-07, R12-03), 4 (TP3-04), 5 (V01-08), and T21-10's note reports 10 on page 376 — one rule with consecutiveBars optimized, default 3. Chose the all-of-N run form over T04-04/T18-05's K-of-N count form as the definition Brooks actually states ('four consecutive large bull trend bars'); the count form is kept separately as StrongTrendBarCount. Per the always-in decision taken by context_regime_always_in, the flip is this rule at consecutiveBars = 2, so V01-08 ('always-in flips after a five-bar spike') needs no separate always-in primitive and is no longer research-grade. TP3-04 and T21-05 also require small tails / little overlap; the tails term is StrongTrendBar's tailFraction and the overlap term is ConsecutiveBarsLittleOverlap, both separate placements.

rules.description: The bar's high-low range is at least K times the N-bar average true range — a climax- or spike-sized bar, identical both sides.

complexity.reason: one ATR window and a comparison

catalog_match.note: BarRangeAboveStd measures the range against an N-bar mean plus K standard deviations; this is a plain ATR multiple, and at K = 5 a far rarer event

rules.merge_notes: V04-07 is a joint volume-and-range climax test; its volume half is the catalog's VolumeAboveAverageMultiple, so only the range half is carried here. Brooks: 'a range that is five or more times larger than most bars of recent days'.

rules.description: The bar opens beyond the prior bar's close in the trend direction — open above the prior close (long) / below it (short): a body-to-body gap and a sign of urgency.
rules.merge_notes: The same one-line test in all four, quoted from the same sentence in two volumes; V02-07 states it as a spike-bar quality test. No thresholds anywhere. Distinct from TrueGapBar, which needs the whole range clear.

rules.description: The pullback since the breakout has not traded back below the breakout bar's high: the lowest low of the last N bars is at or above the high of the bar N bars ago; mirrored for shorts.

complexity.reason: one window extreme against a fixed-offset bar high

rules.merge_notes: T19-07 persists a breakout bar's high; T00-37's fixed window won — the bar testWindow bars back stands in for the breakout bar, so no state is carried. R08-11 anchors on the broken N-bar high instead of the breakout bar's own high; recorded, bar-high anchor kept.

rules.description: Each of the last N bars is a bull trend bar (close above open) that also opened above the prior bar's close — a run of body gaps; mirrored for bears.
rules.pseudocode: for i in 0..consecutiveBars-1: open[i] > close[i+1] && close[i] > open[i]

catalog_match.note: ConsecutiveUpBars counts close-above-open bars only; this adds the open-above-prior-close gap to every bar of the run

rules.merge_notes: Only R06-03 states the run form ('two or three of these gaps on consecutive bull trend bars'); default 2. Kept apart from BodyGapBar, the one-bar test, per the one-bar-versus-run rule.

rules.description: The bar gaps and the gap is larger than a fraction of the recent average bar range — Brooks's second 'large gap' test.
rules.pseudocode: low[0] > high[1] && (low[0] - high[1]) >= gapRangeFraction * average(high - low, rangeLookback)

complexity.reason: a windowed average of high-low against the derived gap size

rules.merge_notes: 'Larger than about half of the average daily range.' rangeLookback 20 is the miner's reading — the book gives no bar count. Kept apart from LargeGapVsRecentGaps, which Brooks gives as the alternative test in the same sentence.

rules.description: The bar gaps and its gap is at least as large as the largest gap of the prior N bars — Brooks's first 'large gap' test.

complexity.reason: a Highest over a derived per-bar gap-size series

rules.merge_notes: Brooks offers two alternative large-gap tests with 'or', so this and LargeGapVsAverageRange stay apart until someone measures that they coincide. Needs a derived signed gap-size series before the Highest window. 'Five days or so' is his own hedge.

rules.description: The prior bar left a micro gap (its low above the high of the bar before it) and this bar pulls back to within X ticks of that gap's lower edge — a with-trend limit entry at the breakout point.
rules.pseudocode: low[1] > high[2] && low[0] <= high[2] + entryOffsetTicks * tickSize

complexity.reason: fixed three-bar offsets plus a tick-offset comparison

rules.merge_notes: R28-03's indexing won: the limit sits above the high of the bar BEFORE the breakout bar (high[2]). R06-15 writes high[1], the breakout bar's own high, contradicting its own quote — a mining slip. Its three-tick risk figure is a stop, not part of this rule.

rules.description: Around a strong bull trend bar, the bar after it does not overlap the bar before it — this bar's low is at or above the high of two bars ago; mirrored for bears.
rules.pseudocode: close[1] > open[1] && (close[1] - open[1]) >= bodyFraction * (high[1] - low[1]) && low[0] >= high[2]

complexity.reason: fixed three-bar arithmetic plus a body-fraction test on the middle bar

rules.merge_notes: Five statements of one three-bar test. R02-22 is its negation, Brooks's matching sign of weakness, so the per-placement negate toggle covers it. bodyFraction 0.7 in V00-15/T00-14/T19-06; R00-26's tick tolerance dropped, its default is 0.

rules.description: The bar's range does not overlap the reference bar's range at all: low is above the high of the bar N bars ago (long) / high below its low (short) — Brooks's plain gap.

catalog_match.note: CloseAbovePriorHigh compares close to high[N]; this needs the whole bar clear of it (low > high[N]), a strictly stronger non-overlap test

rules.merge_notes: Four identical statements of non-overlap. VP1-31's gapBarOffset input kept, default 1. R08-04 and V20-01 both say the same test runs unchanged on daily bars ('on any time frame'), hence timeframe daily-ok.

rules.description: Exit the long when the close falls back below the lower edge of the most recent bull gap inside the lookback (the high of the bar before the gap); mirrored for shorts.
rules.pseudocode: k = smallest j in 1..gapLookback with low[j] > high[j+1]; gapBottom = high[k+1]; close[0] < gapBottom

complexity.reason: bounded backward scan for the most recent gap; no persistent state once the scan is bounded

rules.merge_notes: R06-08 only. Brooks anchors on 'the identified gap'; mechanized as a bounded backward scan for the most recent TrueGapBar, which avoids carrying gap state. Its tick tolerance is dropped (source default 0). Brooks reads the fill as exhaustion, a buy climax.
